title: Introduction to Causal Inference
description: Causal inference is a vital tool for understanding the complex relationships between variables. Distinguishing between correlation and causation is essential for making informed decisions in policy, business, and research. By employing robust methodologies, researchers can draw meaningful conclusions that enhance our understanding of the world and guide effective actions.

title: Methods of Causal Inference
description: Selecting the appropriate method depends on the specific research question, available resources, and ethical considerations. Often, researchers may combine multiple methodologies to strengthen their causal claims, thereby enhancing the robustness and reliability of their findings.

title: The Role of Counterfactuals in Causal Inference
description: Counterfactual reasoning plays a vital role in the design of studies by guiding researchers in defining their treatment and control groups, as well as the outcomes they aim to measure. Here are several ways counterfactuals inform study design
keywords: The Role of Counterfactuals in Causal Inference

title: Causal Graphs and Diagrams
description: Causal graphs and diagrams are powerful tools in causal inference, providing a visual representation of the relationships between variables. They clarify assumptions, illustrate causal pathways, and guide the analysis of complex systems.

title: Machine Learning and Causal Inference
description: y combining the predictive power of machine learning with rigorous causal methods, researchers can harness the strengths of both fields to produce reliable and insightful causal inferences. Balancing prediction with causal rigor will be key to the successful application of machine learning in causal research.

title: Natural Experiments in Causal Analysis
description: Natural experiments provide a valuable alternative to randomized controlled trials in situations where randomization is impractical or unethical. By carefully selecting events, policies, or natural variations that approximate random assignment, researchers can make credible causal inferences about real-world phenomena.

title: Causal inference overview | comparision with ab test
description: A/B testing relies on random assignment to control and treatment groups to directly measure causal effects in a controlled environment, primarily used for experiments like marketing or product testing. In contrast, causal inference can analyze observational data without randomized experiments, often applying more complex statistical methods to estimate causal relationships when controlled experiments are impractical. Both aim to identify cause-effect relationships, but A/B testing is more straightforward due to randomization, while causal inference handles more complex, non-experimental data.
